## What every acoustic measure sees

Every acoustic measure in this reference is computed on a digital signal: a
sequence of numbers that stands for the continuous pressure waveform at the
microphone. The path from a sustained vowel to a jitter or CPPS value passes
through five stages.

1. **Sampling** discretises time.
2. **Quantization** discretises amplitude.
3. **Framing** cuts the sample stream into short segments.
4. **Windowing** tapers each segment before spectral analysis.
5. **Transformation** moves the frame into the frequency or cepstral domain.

Sampling and quantization together are the essence of digitization
[@kent2002acoustic, p. 62]. Each stage has parameters (sampling rate, bit
depth, frame length, window shape) that limit what a downstream measure can
report. Every measure chapter names the parameters it presupposes, and this
chapter is where those names are defined.

## Continuous and discrete signals

A continuous-time signal has a value at every instant. A discrete-time signal
has values only at chosen instants, and can be derived from a continuous one
by sampling [@ludlow2018measuring, p. 4]. The operation that turns the
microphone's analog signal into a series of stored numbers is
analog-to-digital (A/D) conversion. The reverse operation, needed to play a
stored signal, is digital-to-analog (D/A) conversion [@kent2002acoustic, p. 63].

In the notation used throughout this reference, the sampled sequence is
$x[n] = x_a(nT)$, where $x_a(t)$ is the analog signal, $n$ is an integer
sample index, and $T$ is the sampling period [@rabiner2011theory, p. 44].
The sampling rate is $F_s = 1/T$.

## Sampling and aliasing

The sampling rate is the number of samples taken per second. A rate of 10 kHz
samples the analog signal 10,000 times per second [@kent2002acoustic, p. 62].

The sampling theorem states the condition for a lossless representation. If
the analog signal contains no energy at or above a frequency $F_N$, it can be
reconstructed uniquely from its samples provided $F_s \ge 2F_N$
[@rabiner2011theory, p. 44]. $F_N$ is the Nyquist frequency and $2F_N$ is the
Nyquist rate [@baken2000clinical, p. 80]. When the condition fails, energy
above half the sampling rate reappears at a lower, false frequency. This error
is called aliasing [@kent2002acoustic, p. 65].

@fig-aliasing repeats a classic demonstration. A 100-Hz sine is sampled at
four rates. At 250 samples/s there are only 2.5 samples per cycle, yet the
100-Hz periodicity survives. At 160 samples/s there are fewer than two samples
per cycle and the samples trace a slower wave [@baken2000clinical, p. 80].

::: {#cell-fig-aliasing .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
f, dur = 100.0, 0.1
t = np.linspace(0, dur, 4000, endpoint=False)
rates = [1000, 500, 250, 160]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(rates) + 1, 1, figsize=(7, 5.6), sharex=True)
axes[0].plot(t * 1e3, np.sin(2 * np.pi * f * t), color=vs.INK, lw=1.4)
axes[0].set_title("Analog signal: 100-Hz sine", color=vs.INK)
for ax, fs in zip(axes[1:], rates):
    n = np.arange(int(dur * fs))
    tn = n / fs
    xn = np.sin(2 * np.pi * f * tn)
    ax.plot(t * 1e3, np.sin(2 * np.pi * f * t), color=vs.GRID, lw=1.0)
    ax.plot(tn * 1e3, xn, color=vs.BLUE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.6)
    ax.plot(tn * 1e3, xn, "o", color=vs.BLUE, ms=4)
    title = f"Sampled at {fs} samples/s  ({fs / f:.1f} samples per cycle)"
    if fs < 2 * f:
        fa = abs(f - fs)
        ax.plot(t * 1e3, -np.sin(2 * np.pi * fa * t), "--", color=vs.ORANGE, lw=1.4)
        title += f": aliased to {fa:.0f} Hz"
    ax.set_title(title, color=vs.INK)
for ax in axes:
    vs.style_axes(ax)
    ax.set_ylim(-1.35, 1.35)
    ax.set_yticks([-1, 0, 1])
axes[-1].set_xlabel("Time (ms)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Choosing a sampling rate

The sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency of interest
[@kent2002acoustic, p. 64]. For voice work the highest frequency of interest
is set by the harmonics and by any noise, not by F0. For a periodic
physiological signal, the highest frequency of interest is usually about
$10F_0$, and sampling a little above the Nyquist rate (about 20 % more) gives
a margin for residual noise [@baken2000clinical, p. 81]. Baken and Orlikoff
recommend at least 20,000 samples/s for speech, and for any signal with
significant aperiodic energy such as turbulence noise
[@baken2000clinical, p. 81]. For archiving, 44.1 kHz with 16-bit depth is
agreed good practice, and 44.1 or 96 kHz with 24-bit depth is best practice
[@ludlow2018measuring, p. 140].

The analysable bandwidth follows from the theorem.

| Sampling rate | Highest analysable frequency ($F_s/2$) | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| 96 kHz | 48 kHz | archival best practice [@ludlow2018measuring, p. 140] |
| 44.1 kHz | 22.05 kHz | archival good practice [@ludlow2018measuring, p. 140] |
| 20 kHz | 10 kHz | recommended minimum for speech [@baken2000clinical, p. 81] |
| 8 kHz | 4 kHz | narrowband telephony [@rabiner2011theory, p. 47] |

### Anti-aliasing filter

A sampling rate that looks adequate is not sufficient on its own. Any energy
above the Nyquist frequency will alias, so the signal must be band-limited by
a low-pass anti-aliasing filter before the A/D converter
[@baken2000clinical, p. 81]. Ordinary low-pass filters roll off too gently for
this purpose. A component one octave above the cutoff may be attenuated by only
about 12 dB, so anti-aliasing filters need very steep roll-offs
[@baken2000clinical, pp. 81--82]. Kent and Read give a working specification:
pass-band ripple below 0.5 dB and stop-band attenuation of at least 68 dB
[@kent2002acoustic, p. 64].

### Pre-emphasis

Most speech analysis chains apply pre-emphasis, a high-frequency boost, before
spectral analysis. Most of the energy of speech lies at low frequencies and
would otherwise dominate the analysis [@kent2002acoustic, p. 63]. Pre-emphasis
is either a filter giving +6 dB/octave above a breakpoint between 100 and
1000 Hz, or first differencing of the samples, $y[n] = x[n] - a\,x[n-1]$
[@kent2002acoustic, pp. 63--64]. The two methods give comparable results. A
system that differences digitally must not also be fed through a hardware
pre-emphasis filter, or the signal is pre-emphasised twice
[@kent2002acoustic, p. 64]. Pre-emphasis settings are one of the parameters
to check when comparing values across software.

## Quantization

Quantization discretises amplitude. Each sample is stored as one of $2^N$
levels, where $N$ is the number of bits [@ludlow2018measuring, p. 4].

| Bits ($N$) | Levels ($2^N$) |
|---|---|
| 8 | 256 |
| 10 | 1,024 |
| 12 | 4,096 |
| 16 | 65,536 |
| 24 | 16,777,216 |

Rounding a smoothly varying signal to discrete levels adds spurious
components called quantization noise. The noise is minimised by using as many
quantization levels as possible [@baken2000clinical, p. 79]. As a rule, each
additional bit adds about 6 dB to the signal-to-quantization-noise ratio
[@rabiner2011theory, p. 688].

Bit depth only helps if the signal uses it. The step size of the converter is
fixed, so a signal that spans a fraction of the input range is quantized with
fewer effective levels. In Baken and Orlikoff's example, a 2-V signal on a
10-bit converter with a 0 to 5 V range uses only 9 of the 10 bits
[@baken2000clinical, p. 79]. Equivalently, a signal that varies over only half
the converter's range loses 6 dB of signal-to-quantization-noise ratio
[@rabiner2011theory, p. 690]. @fig-quantization shows the effect.

::: {#cell-fig-quantization .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fs = 16000
per = np.full(8, 1 / 125)
x = vs.synth_vowel(per, np.ones(8), fs)[: int(0.016 * fs)]
t = np.arange(len(x)) / fs * 1e3
bits = 4
step = 2 / 2 ** bits  # full range is -1..+1

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(7, 4.2), sharex=True,
                         gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2.2, 1]})
for col, gain in enumerate([0.98, 0.245]):
    xs = gain * x
    xq = np.clip(np.round(xs / step) * step, -1, 1 - step)
    top, bot = axes[0, col], axes[1, col]
    for lev in np.arange(-1, 1 + 1e-9, step):
        top.axhline(lev, color=vs.GRID, lw=0.5, zorder=0)
    top.plot(t, xs, color=vs.MUTED, lw=1.2)
    top.step(t, xq, where="mid", color=vs.BLUE, lw=1.1)
    top.set_ylim(-1.05, 1.05)
    top.set_title(("Full scale" if col == 0 else "One quarter of full scale")
                  + f", {bits} bits", color=vs.INK)
    bot.plot(t, xs - xq, color=vs.ORANGE, lw=0.9)
    bot.set_ylim(-step, step)
    bot.set_xlabel("Time (ms)")
    vs.style_axes(top, grid=False)
    vs.style_axes(bot)
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("Amplitude (full scale = ±1)")
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("Error")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

How many bits are enough depends on the measure and on the era of the
recommendation. Baken and Orlikoff judged 12 bits adequate for clinical needs
[@baken2000clinical, p. 79], and treat 10 bits as the minimum for shimmer
measurement [@baken2000clinical, p. 132]. Current archival practice records at
16 or 24 bits [@ludlow2018measuring, p. 140]. The practical rule is the same in
every source that discusses it: amplify the signal so that its largest peaks
are just below the converter's maximum input [@baken2000clinical, p. 79].

Going past the maximum is worse than staying well below it. An amplifier or
converter driven beyond its range flattens the tops of the waveform. This
peak clipping is one of the most common errors made by novices, and it can
make a speech recording unsuitable for analysis even when the distortion is
hard to see [@baken2000clinical, p. 57].

## Short-time analysis: frames and windows

Speech properties change slowly compared with the sample-to-sample detail of
the waveform, at rates on the order of 10 to 30 times per second. Short-time
analysis exploits this: it isolates short segments (frames) and processes each
as if it came from a sustained sound with fixed properties
[@rabiner2011theory, p. 242]. Successive frames overlap to keep the analysis
continuous, and each frame is multiplied by a window that reduces the effect
of the abrupt cut at its edges [@ludlow2018measuring, p. 168].

::: {#cell-fig-framing .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fs = 16000
x = vs.synth_vowel(np.full(20, 1 / 125), np.ones(20), fs)[: int(0.08 * fs)]
t = np.arange(len(x)) / fs * 1e3
L, H = int(0.030 * fs), int(0.010 * fs)
w = np.hamming(L)
starts = [int(0.015 * fs) + k * H for k in range(3)]
colors = [vs.BLUE, vs.ORANGE, vs.GREEN]

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7, 4.2), sharex=True)
a1.plot(t, x, color=vs.MUTED, lw=0.9)
for k, (s, c) in enumerate(zip(starts, colors)):
    tt = t[s:s + L]
    a1.plot(tt, w * 1.05, color=c, lw=1.6)
    a1.text(tt[L // 2], 1.12, f"frame {k + 1}", color=vs.INK, ha="center", fontsize=8.5)
a1.set_ylim(-1.1, 1.3)
a1.set_title("Overlapping frames (30 ms long, 10 ms hop)", color=vs.INK)
s = starts[1]
a2.plot(t, np.zeros_like(t), color=vs.GRID, lw=0.8)
a2.plot(t[s:s + L], x[s:s + L] * w, color=vs.ORANGE, lw=1.1)
a2.set_title("Frame 2 after Hamming windowing", color=vs.INK)
a2.set_xlabel("Time (ms)")
for ax in (a1, a2):
    vs.style_axes(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Frame length

No single frame length is ideal. A frame on the order of one pitch period or
shorter makes short-time measures fluctuate with the exact waveform detail. A
frame of tens of pitch periods changes too slowly to follow the signal. Pitch
periods range from about 2 ms (500 Hz, a child or high female voice) to about
12.5 ms (80 Hz, a very low male voice). Rabiner and Schafer therefore suggest
frames of 10 to 40 ms with 50 to 75 % overlap between successive frames
[@rabiner2011theory, p. 248]. Ludlow, Kent and Gray describe frames on the
order of 25 to 50 ms, long enough to include at least two pitch periods of a
man's voice [@ludlow2018measuring, p. 168].

### Window shape

The window shape controls how energy at one frequency leaks into its
neighbours. The Hamming window used by most voice software is

$$
w[n] = 0.54 - 0.46 \cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi n}{N-1}\right), \qquad 0 \le n \le N-1
$$

[@rabiner2011theory, p. 57]. Two properties of a window's spectrum matter: the
width of its main lobe and the height of its side lobes. The main-lobe width is
inversely proportional to the window length, while the side-lobe level depends
mainly on the window shape [@rabiner2011theory, p. 297].

| Window | Main-lobe width (length $L$ samples) | Highest side lobe | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rectangular | about $2F_s/L$ | about 14 dB below the main lobe | [@rabiner2011theory, p. 297] |
| Hamming | about $4F_s/L$ | 40 dB or more below the main lobe | [@rabiner2011theory, p. 298] |

For the same length, the rectangular window has half the main-lobe width of
the Hamming window, but its large side lobes let strong harmonics leak across
the spectrum and offset that advantage [@rabiner2011theory, pp. 302--303].
@fig-windows shows both windows and their spectra.

::: {#cell-fig-windows .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fs = 16000
L = int(0.030 * fs)
nfft = 2 ** 16
wins = {"Rectangular": (np.ones(L), vs.ORANGE), "Hamming": (np.hamming(L), vs.BLUE)}
f = np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fftfreq(nfft, 1 / fs))

fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 3.0), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.5]})
for name, (w, c) in wins.items():
    a1.plot(np.arange(L) / fs * 1e3, w, color=c, lw=1.6, label=name)
    W = np.fft.fftshift(np.abs(np.fft.fft(w, nfft)))
    WdB = 20 * np.log10(W / W.max() + 1e-12)
    a2.plot(f, WdB, color=c, lw=1.3, label=name)
a1.set_xlabel("Time (ms)")
a1.set_ylim(-0.25, 1.1)
a1.set_title("Windows", color=vs.INK)
a2.set_xlim(-400, 400)
a2.set_ylim(-80, 3)
a2.set_xlabel("Frequency offset (Hz)")
a2.set_ylabel("Magnitude (dB)")
a2.set_title("Window spectra", color=vs.INK)
for lvl in (-13.3, -42.7):
    a2.axhline(lvl, color=vs.MUTED, lw=0.7, ls=":")
a2.text(-395, -11.5, "−13 dB", ha="left", fontsize=8, color=vs.INK)
a2.text(-395, -41, "−43 dB", ha="left", fontsize=8, color=vs.INK)
a1.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8.5, loc="lower center")
for ax in (a1, a2):
    vs.style_axes(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Narrowband and wideband analysis

Frame length decides whether the analysis resolves harmonics or glottal
cycles. When the window spans several pitch periods, its main lobe is narrower
than the harmonic spacing and each harmonic appears as a separate peak. This is
narrowband analysis. When the window spans about one pitch period, harmonics
are not resolved, but individual glottal periods are resolved in time. This is
wideband analysis [@rabiner2011theory, p. 299].

Rabiner and Schafer's worked example makes the numbers concrete. A 31.25-ms
Hamming window has a main lobe about 128 Hz wide. That is narrower than the
148-Hz F0 of their speaker, so the harmonics separate
[@rabiner2011theory, p. 299]. The same arithmetic shows why a 30-ms Hamming
window does not resolve harmonics below about 130 Hz cleanly: $4/0.030 \approx
133$ Hz. Longer windows are needed for low voices.

::: {#cell-fig-nb-wb .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fs = 16000
dur = 0.35
f0 = np.linspace(110, 200, 400)
periods, tcur = [], 0.0
while tcur < dur + 0.05:
    p = 1 / np.interp(tcur, np.linspace(0, dur, 400), f0)
    periods.append(p)
    tcur += p
x = vs.synth_vowel(np.array(periods), np.ones(len(periods)), fs, noise_rel_db=-40)[: int(dur * fs)]
x = np.append(x[0], x[1:] - 0.94 * x[:-1])  # pre-emphasis for display

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 3.1), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, wl) in zip(axes, [("Narrowband: 40-ms window", 0.040),
                                  ("Wideband: 4-ms window", 0.004)]):
    vs.plot_spectrogram(ax, x, fs, win_s=wl, fmax=4000, hop_s=0.0005, dyn_db=60)
    ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
    ax.set_title(name, color=vs.INK)
    vs.style_axes(ax, grid=False)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Frequency (kHz)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Right, wideband (4 ms): harmonics merge into formant bands, and the vertical striations are individual glottal cycles.](foundations-signal_files/figure-html/fig-nb-wb-output-1.png){#fig-nb-wb width=760 height=330 fig-alt='Two spectrograms from 0 to 4 kHz over 0.35 seconds. ## Time, frequency, and cepstral domains

Periodicity has an exact definition. A waveform $f(t)$ is periodic with period
$T$ when $f(t + T) = f(t)$ for every $t$: the waveform is an exact copy of
itself after $T$ seconds [@titze2000principles, p. 96]. Periodicity in time and
harmonicity in frequency are the same property seen from the two sides of the
time-frequency relation [@titze2000principles, p. 95]. Voice measures look for
this property in one of three domains (@fig-domains).

**Time domain.** The sample sequence $x[n]$ itself. Waveform display, F0
analysis, and jitter and shimmer analysis work here [@kent2002acoustic, p. 62].

**Frequency domain.** The magnitude of the discrete Fourier transform of a
windowed frame is its short-time spectrum; a sequence of such spectra is a
spectrogram. Spectrograms, FFT and LPC spectra, and signal-to-noise
computations work here [@kent2002acoustic, p. 62].

**Cepstral domain.** The cepstrum of a discrete-time signal is the inverse
Fourier transform of the logarithm of the magnitude of its Fourier transform.
Its independent variable is called quefrency, and it has units of time
[@rabiner2011theory, p. 399]. For a voiced frame, the cepstrum has a peak at the
quefrency equal to the pitch period. A strong peak signals voicing, and its
position estimates the period [@rabiner2011theory, p. 425]. Cepstral peak
prominence measures the height of this peak; see the [CPPS chapter](cpps.qmd).

::: {#cell-fig-domains .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fs = 16000
f0 = 125.0
x = vs.synth_vowel(np.full(12, 1 / f0), np.ones(12), fs, noise_rel_db=-40)
L = int(0.040 * fs)
fr = x[int(0.02 * fs): int(0.02 * fs) + L] * np.hamming(L)
nfft = 4096
X = np.fft.rfft(fr, nfft)
logmag = 20 * np.log10(np.abs(X) + 1e-9)
freq = np.fft.rfftfreq(nfft, 1 / fs)
ceps = np.fft.irfft(logmag, nfft)
q = np.arange(nfft) / fs * 1e3
qmin, qmax = int(fs / 400), int(fs / 60)
pk = qmin + np.argmax(ceps[qmin:qmax])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(7, 6.0))
t = np.arange(L) / fs * 1e3
axes[0].plot(t, x[int(0.02 * fs): int(0.02 * fs) + L], color=vs.INK, lw=1.0)
seg = x[int(0.02 * fs): int(0.02 * fs) + L]
p1 = int(np.argmax(seg[: int(fs / f0)]))  # largest peak in the first cycle
t1, t2 = t[p1] + 1e3 / f0, t[p1] + 2e3 / f0
axes[0].annotate("", xy=(t1, 1.1), xytext=(t2, 1.1),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=vs.ORANGE, lw=1.2))
axes[0].text((t1 + t2) / 2, 1.17, "T = 8 ms", ha="center", color=vs.INK, fontsize=8.5)
axes[0].set_ylim(-1.1, 1.35)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Time (ms)")
axes[0].set_title("Time domain: waveform", color=vs.INK)

axes[1].plot(freq, logmag - logmag.max(), color=vs.BLUE, lw=0.9)
axes[1].set_xlim(0, 4000)
axes[1].set_ylim(-70, 3)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("dB")
axes[1].set_title("Frequency domain: log-magnitude spectrum", color=vs.INK)

axes[2].plot(q, ceps, color=vs.GREEN, lw=0.9)
axes[2].plot(q[pk], ceps[pk], "o", color=vs.ORANGE, ms=6)
axes[2].annotate(f"peak at {q[pk]:.1f} ms  (= 1/F0)", xy=(q[pk], ceps[pk]),
                 xytext=(q[pk] + 2, ceps[pk] * 0.85), fontsize=8.5, color=vs.INK)
axes[2].set_xlim(1, 20)
axes[2].set_ylim(ceps[qmin:int(0.02 * fs)].min() * 1.1, ceps[pk] * 1.25)
axes[2].set_xlabel("Quefrency (ms)")
axes[2].set_title("Cepstral domain: cepstrum", color=vs.INK)
for ax in axes:
    vs.style_axes(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

When the periodicity condition fails badly, measures that depend on a period
lose their meaning. The [Signal Typing chapter](foundations-signal-typing.qmd)
describes how to recognise such signals before measuring them.

## Sampling rate and cycle-level measures

Jitter and shimmer are computed cycle by cycle, not frame by frame, so they
have their own digitisation limits. A cycle boundary can be located only to
within one sampling interval, $1/F_s$. That error is fixed while the period
shortens as F0 rises, so the relative error grows in proportion to F0
[@baken2000clinical, p. 193]. Baken and Orlikoff give the maximum jitter error
due to sampling, after Titze, Horii and Scherer (1987), as
$\pm 50\,F_0/F_s$ percent. At 25,000 samples/s this is 0.2 % for a 100-Hz voice
and 0.6 % for a 300-Hz voice, which they call large compared with the jitter
expected in a normal voice [@baken2000clinical, p. 194].

| Mean F0 | Max. error at 25 kHz | at 44.1 kHz | at 96 kHz |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 Hz | 0.20 % | 0.11 % | 0.05 % |
| 200 Hz | 0.40 % | 0.23 % | 0.10 % |
| 300 Hz | 0.60 % | 0.34 % | 0.16 % |

: Maximum jitter error from the relation $\pm 50\,F_0/F_s$ %. The 25-kHz column is given by @baken2000clinical [p. 194]; the other columns apply the same relation. {#tbl-jitter-error}

Interpolation between samples greatly reduces this limitation and makes
ordinary sampling rates adequate for everyday practice
[@baken2000clinical, p. 194]. Sample size also matters. For normal voices,
as few as 30 consecutive cycles may be adequate for a jitter estimate
[@baken2000clinical, p. 194], and at least 30 consecutive cycles should be
included for shimmer [@baken2000clinical, p. 132]. For shimmer, any low-pass
filter should have its cutoff at least one octave above F0, because filtering
alters peak amplitudes [@baken2000clinical, p. 132].

## Caveats

- **Software defaults differ.** Different analysis systems can return
  different jitter and shimmer values for the same signal, and software
  characteristics do not account for all of the variability
  [@baken2000clinical, pp. 132, 194]. Frame length, window, pre-emphasis and
  interpolation are all candidates. Report the software and its settings with
  every value.
- **Check the whole chain, not only the file header.** A file saved at a high
  sampling rate is only as good as the anti-aliasing filter and the gain
  setting used when it was recorded [@baken2000clinical, pp. 79, 81].
- **Clipping cannot be undone.** Peak clipping removes waveform detail at
  recording time [@baken2000clinical, p. 57]. Inspect every recording for
  flattened peaks before analysis.
- **Frame length is a choice with consequences.** A window long enough to
  resolve the harmonics of a low voice smears fast changes, and a short one
  does the reverse [@rabiner2011theory, pp. 248, 299]. Measure chapters state
  the frame length each measure assumes.

## Points of disagreement

The sources give different numerical recommendations for the same parameters.
The differences reflect their dates and purposes rather than a conflict about
the underlying theory.

| Parameter | Recommendation | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Frame length | 10--40 ms, 50--75 % overlap (general speech processing) | @rabiner2011theory [p. 248] |
| Frame length | 25--50 ms, at least two periods of a male voice | @ludlow2018measuring [p. 168] |
| Bit depth | 12 bits meets clinical needs | @baken2000clinical [p. 79] |
| Bit depth | 10 bits minimum for shimmer | @baken2000clinical [p. 132] |
| Bit depth | 16 bits good practice; 24 bits best practice (archiving) | @ludlow2018measuring [p. 140] |
| Sampling rate | at least 20 kHz for speech | @baken2000clinical [p. 81] |
| Sampling rate | 44.1 kHz good practice; 44.1 or 96 kHz best practice (archiving) | @ludlow2018measuring [p. 140] |
